Every cell of E43 was then rerun; the 610 earlier rows are archived and reproducible with the fix off. Against the 610 archived rows with the same cell and seed, the primary outcome moved by −0.13 h on average and by 3.8 h in absolute value, with a largest single-run change of 43 h (in the uncoordinated mode, whose hand-resolution waits depend on the order of events); 69 % of the rows moved by more than 0.1 h. P2-ID-FIX-SENTENCE: After every experiment had run, a verification check found that cargo ids were not unique: 9–18 of about 2,970 items a year reused an earlier id, in every regime (change 10 of the pre-registration). Ids enter the simulator's decisions only through a planning memo within one dispatch call. The fix was tested by rerunning 48 full years (E40, E43: every regime or mode, seeds 1–3), of which 48 gave outcomes identical item by item, compared by content without ids, 9 of them in this paper's experiment; reused ids fell from 670 to 0. No experiment was rerun and no reported number changes; trace and scene files written before the fix still carry the duplicate ids.
P2-CHECK-FINDINGS-SENTENCE: Of the failures, S1 (c) type 9, non-conforming (58 violations) and S5 encounter deadlocks (390 encounters) are the findings of Section 5.6, type 9's violations beyond the leader-braking assumption and the deadlocks of change 9. The S2 row flags the shield's one accepted unsafe case: of 1,000 injected proposals to brake on a slope that friction cannot hold, 990 were refused and 10 accepted, all at near-standstill, a case that R2 keeps every run from reaching (Section 7). The T3 row against the continuous saturation-flow formula fails by 1.7 % (609 against 620 vehicles an hour), because the shield's one-step look-ahead keeps a longer following gap than the formula's minimum; the row with that look-ahead in the formula matches to 0.01 %.
P2-SHIELD-SLOPE-SENTENCE: The phase-5 check S2 injected 1,000 proposals to brake on a slope steeper than friction can hold and the shield refused 990; the 10 it accepted were vehicles at near-standstill, because the shield's kinematics take a stopped vehicle to stay stopped. R2 never admits a vehicle to such a slope, so no run of E43, E44 or E47 reaches the case, and the shield was not changed after the runs; a flight implementation should flag it.
P2-PAIRING-SENTENCE: The engine's phase-5 check D10 (Section 3.8) confirms the pairing on the companion paper's regimes: the demand stream, landings and manifests, was identical across 880 regime pairs on the same seed and start year, while the per-job intervention and fault redraws, shared in draw order, diverge once the allocations differ; E43's modes draw from the same streams, so a pair shares its year and diverges in those draws after the first conflict.
P2-DEADLOCK-SCOPE-CLAUSE: That zero is a property of the logistics model rather than of the rule: its bays are unbounded and its reservation table is filled one job at a time (Section 3.4), so no circular wait can form there, and the count is a check of the code. With finite bays the exit-bay rule is not deadlock-free on a ring of single-lane segments, as the encounter simulator's ring type shows (Section 5.6), and whether this base has such a ring the 5 m route samples cannot settle: merged to road nodes within 40 m they show one candidate ring of 419 m at the default share, one at a 5 % share and 14 at 40 %, but the merge can itself join neighbouring roads, and before merging the 5 loops at the default share are one road sampled twice by different legs. A surveyed centreline map would settle it; the samples do not.
P2-E44-DESIGN-SENTENCE: Types 1 and 7 run 100,000 encounters each and the other ten 10,000 (change 6 of [43], a cost of compute on the shared machine that weakens those bounds tenfold); type-1 draws whose slope and friction cannot hold the vehicle (25 % of them) are not driven and are counted apart. Each type's bound is the 95 % upper limit on the probability of a hard violation under that type's parameter distribution: with no violation 1 − 0.05<sup>1/n<sub>eff</sub></sup> and, beside it, the Bonferroni limit 1 − (0.05/12)<sup>1/n<sub>eff</sub></sup> over the twelve types; with violations the Clopper–Pearson upper limit on the unweighted count at the same levels, with the limit on the weighted violation share at the effective n reported beside it. Types 6, 7 and 9 are importance-sampled (the inside vehicle's exit distance, the crew's emergence time and the dead-stop time) with weights p/q and an effective n of (Σw)<sup>2</sup>/Σw<sup>2</sup>; type 12 fuzzes draws of types 1, 2, 4 and 7 and so inherits type 1's undriven slopes and type 7's weights. A near miss is a same-lane gap below twice d<sub>min</sub>, a time to collision below 10 s, a crew clearance below twice the stopping radius, or a zone exit margin below 300 s; the minimum margin is the smallest clearance to another vehicle or crew member. Every encounter receives exactly one of six outcomes by precedence (not driven, violation, blocked by a fault, deadlock, finished, incomplete); deadlock is judged only where no random fuzzer runs, and an emergency-brake event (no candidate satisfies every rule and the shield applies full braking) is a rate, not an outcome. The first main run was stopped when two simulator defects showed as violations, the vehicle body swinging off the path at corners and type-6 crossings built without a junction tile; both were fixed, the stored encounters regenerated and all twelve types rerun at the same n (change 8 of [43]); the stopped run's counts are reported in Section 5.6 and its files archived. During the rerun the type-6 cell ran three times: its first pass showed a third defect, start states inside a vehicle's own stopping distance of a crossing tile, and a same-lane test in the gap metric wide enough to count two vehicles leaving a shallow crossing on different roads; its second pass exposed a stall classifier that counted a vehicle correctly held at a closed zone as waiting for a grant. The builder and the classifier were fixed, the metric's same-lane test narrowed to the same road and direction (the shield's own leader test is unchanged), and types 3, 5 and 6 rerun at the same n so that every count is under the one final metric and classifier (change 9 of [43]). Twenty stored encounters must reproduce exactly on every build.
P2-E44-DESIGN-SENTENCE-SHORT: 300,000 encounters in the twelve types of Table 3 (100,000 in types 1 and 7, 10,000 in each other), with the three planners of Section 3.5, importance weights on types 6, 7 and 9, and a 95 % per-type bound with a Bonferroni correction over the types.
P2-E44-INTRO-CLAUSE: In 274,580 driven encounters of twelve types the safety program allowed no hard violation in eleven types, with a bound on the violation probability of 1.2 × 10<sup>−3</sup> or less, jointly at 95 % over the twelve types, under each type's parameter distribution; the exception is a vehicle that stops dead inside a one-lane segment (type 9), where the following vehicle closed below the required gap in 58 of 10,000 encounters and touched it in 7, because the gap rule assumes a leader that brakes rather than stops (Section 5.6).
P2-E44-RESULTS-PARAGRAPH: Table 6 gives every type. Of the 300,000 encounters generated, 274,580 were driven (24,743 type-1 draws and 677 type-12 draws could not hold the vehicle on the slope). Eleven of the twelve types produced no hard violation in 264,580 driven encounters; their Bonferroni bounds run from 7.3 × 10<sup>−5</sup> (type 1, following, effective n 75,257) to 1.2 × 10<sup>−3</sup> (type 6, the landing closure, effective n 4,545). Type 9 (the nonconforming vehicle) had 58 violating encounters in 10,000 (effective n 6,115): 7 contacts, 58 below the required gap; an encounter may count under more than one kind. Its Clopper–Pearson upper limit is 8.1 × 10<sup>−3</sup> on the unweighted count and 9.2 × 10<sup>−3</sup> on its weighted violation share (0.61 %) at the effective n. Every one of them is in the dead-stop bin, where a fault stops the leader instantly; the slip and drift bins of the same type produced none (Section 6.1). H7 as registered, zero violations in every type, is therefore not supported: eleven types produced no violation, of which nine were also free of deadlocks; types 5 and 6 are clean of violations but not live (below). The importance weights reduce the effective n to 4,545 of 10,000 in type 6, 47,148 of 100,000 in type 7, 6,115 of 10,000 in type 9, 7,231 of 9,323 in type 12. Near misses, mostly a same-lane gap under twice d<sub>min</sub>, occurred in 121,468 encounters (44 % of those driven); the smallest clearance in any type without a violation was 1.1 m. Deadlocks occurred in 386 of 10,000 type-5 encounters (3.9 %, the ring of one-lane segments with finite bays), 4 of 10,000 type-6 encounters (the landing closure) and in no other type. The four type-6 deadlocks are all at the 1,000 m zone radius, and a trace of each shows one common cause, a crossing that lies on the zone boundary (Section 6.1). A fault blocked 4,137 type-9 encounters before any rule was tested. The emergency brake fired in up to 52.7 % of a type's encounters (type 7, crew). The first main run, stopped after types 1–10 and part of type 11, had shown 37 violations in type 4, 3 violations in type 5, 82 violations in type 6, 58 violations in type 9 and none elsewhere. Of the violating encounters without a random fuzzer, which are deterministic and can be rerun as they were, 10 of 27 in type 4, 3 of 3 in type 5, 5 of 46 in type 6 were rerun after the fix and every one was clean (spot checks of the first few in batch order under a time budget, superseded by the full rerun at the registered n); 25 of 48 in type 9 were rerun after both fixes and every one still violated (25 below the gap, 4 contacts). The stopped run's files are archived and used for nothing else. The type-6 cell was run three times. Its first pass showed 10 R3 violations, vehicles that started inside their own stopping distance of a crossing tile, a start the protocol never faces, 10 gap counts between vehicles leaving a shallow crossing on different roads with 2.2 m or more between their bodies and no contact, and 201 encounters classed as deadlocks. The first was fixed in the builder and the second by narrowing the gap metric's same-lane test (same road and direction instead of 30°; the shield's leader test is unchanged). No violation count in any other type changes under the narrower test, and type 9's reproduced exactly; the near-miss counts of type 5 and the minimum-gap diagnostic of type 3 did change, so types 3 and 5 were rerun in full under the final metric. The second pass, with both corrections, had no violation and 202 encounters classed as deadlocks; a trace showed slow haulers correctly held at the closed zone, stopped just short of its line, that the stall check counted as waiting for a grant. The classifier was corrected (the deadlock flag and, in type 6, where the stall test ends an encounter; no violation changed) and types 5 and 6 rerun. The third pass is the one reported: type 6 fell from 202 deadlocks to the four above, and type 5's ring deadlocks stand at 386 (change 9 of [43]). Between the second and third passes an exploratory type-6 cell with an added request rule, registered in change 9 against a mechanism that the trace then withdrew, ran once (203 deadlocks against 202) and tested nothing; it is archived with the earlier passes and used for nothing else.
P2-E44-DISCUSSION-CLAUSE: The simulator's one failure is where the derivation says it should be. R1's gap is computed for a leader that brakes at b<sub>max</sub>, and a vehicle that stops dead, a fault rather than a manoeuvre, lies outside that model [14], so a same-direction follower already inside a one-lane segment can close below the gap and, in 7 of 10,000 encounters, touch. A dead-stop margin, the follower's own stopping distance at its current speed, would close the case at a cost in segment capacity; we did not run it, and the count stands as a limit of braking-based separation. The ring deadlocks of type 5 (3.9 % of its encounters) are the property noted before the main run [43]: the exit-bay rule is not deadlock-free on a ring of one-lane segments with finite bays, and the logistics model's zero count comes from its unbounded bays; the count stood when the stall classifier was corrected (change 9 of [43]). The four deadlocks of type 6 are a gap in the rules: a crossing that lies on a landing zone's boundary can be held by a vehicle stopped at the zone line, and the vehicle leaving the closing zone through it is blocked. R3 keeps a vehicle out of a segment it cannot leave into a bay, but no rule keeps it out of a junction whose far side is a hold point. The repair is a one-line extension of R3's exit check to junctions; we did not run it, and the count stands as found.
P2-E44-COMPARISON-CLAUSE: Our per-type bounds are the zero-numerator bounds of Hanley and Lippman-Hand [33]: with no violation in n encounters the 95 % upper limit is close to 3/n, 3.0 × 10<sup>−5</sup> at 100,000 and 3.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> at 10,000, larger at the smaller effective n of the weighted types, and they hold for the generated distribution of each type, not for the base's actual traffic. Zhao and colleagues reach rarer events by importance sampling on the lane-change parameters [35]; we used the same device on three types (the exit distance, the crew's emergence time and the dead-stop time), which cost effective sample size (Section 5.6) and found the one violating case, type 9, where the boosted region was.
P2-E44-COMPUTE-SENTENCE: E44's final run took 9.4 h of processor time in resumable batches of 250 to 4,000 encounters, type 11 the longest at 2.7 h, with a process peak of 136 MB.
P2-E45-DESIGN-SENTENCE: Four layouts of the discrete model of Section 3.6: a pad visit with one oncoming vehicle (landing, crew and radio links); three vehicles on the line, two of them interchangeable (crew, no landing); a pad visit with two oncoming vehicles (landing and crew); a pad visit with two oncoming vehicles and radio links. Then the three mutations, R3 without the exit-slot check, R5 without the entry check, R7 without the hold, each required to produce a counterexample on the layout where the rule acts.
P2-E45-INTRO-CLAUSE: The exhaustive search of the discrete model found no unsafe state, no deadlock and no livelock in 47,085 reachable states over four layouts, every state could reach the goal within 41 steps, and each of three removed rules produced a counterexample (Section 5.7).
P2-E45-RESULTS-PARAGRAPH: The four layouts have 47,085 reachable states and 272,899 transitions in all; the largest, a pad visit with two oncoming vehicles and radio links, has 36,912 states. In every layout the search found no state that breaks a safety invariant, no deadlock state, no state from which the goal is unreachable and no livelock component; the longest shortest path to the goal is 41 steps of 8.5 s on 10 m cells. Each mutation produced its counterexample. Without R3's exit-slot check, 2 reachable states of the three-vehicle line are deadlocks and 39 cannot reach the goal (13 livelock components); the shortest deadlock trace is 12 steps. Without R5's entry check, 384 reachable states have a vehicle inside the landing zone while it is closed, the shortest reached in 14 steps. Without R7's hold, 198 reachable states break an invariant (138 in the segment without the reservation, 96 opposite directions in the segment; a state may break both), the shortest in 5 steps. The traces are stored beside the results. H7's second clause, a counterexample for each removed rule, holds. Development of the checker found four counterexamples before the final run, three in the checker itself (R6 checked as a state invariant rather than on the vehicle's motion, which flagged crew walking up to a stopped vehicle; no crew distance computed on the landing spur, 80 violating states in the first layout; bay slots counted per lane, which hid the R3 mutation) and one in the reading of a rule: with the bays fixed, the three-vehicle line deadlocked when a vehicle granted the segment with a free exit slot lost that slot to a vehicle that drove into the bay afterwards. R3's “reserved for it” therefore binds every other vehicle: a bay counts the slots reserved by segment holders as taken, in the checker and in the encounter simulator alike.
P2-E45-DISCUSSION-CLAUSE: the exhaustive check says that the rules are consistent on every layout the checker can hold, 47,085 states of up to three vehicles on one segment with its bays, a pad and a crew member, and that each of the three clauses we removed is load-bearing: without it the search finds an unsafe or a stuck state within a few steps. It says nothing about larger layouts, which is where the simulator takes over.
P2-E45-COMPUTE-SENTENCE: E45's four layouts and three mutations took 50 s in all, the largest layout 37 s and 29 MB.
P2-H7-ABSTRACT-CLAUSE: The safety program allowed no violation in eleven of twelve encounter types; the exception, a vehicle stopping dead in a one-lane segment, defeats a gap rule derived for a braking leader; the ring of one-lane segments with finite bays deadlocked in 3.9 % of its encounters, and the landing closure four times in 10,000 at a crossing on the zone boundary. The exhaustive search of 47,085 reachable states found no unsafe or stuck state and caught three removed rules.
P2-CONCLUSION-SAFETY-CLAUSE: The exhaustive check found no unsafe or stuck state in 47,085 reachable states; the simulator found no violation in eleven of twelve encounter types, one in the twelfth, a vehicle that stops dead inside a one-lane segment; the ring of one-lane segments with finite bays deadlocked in 3.9 % of its encounters, and the landing closure four times in 10,000 at a crossing on the zone boundary.
P2-E47-DESIGN-SENTENCE: E44's twelve types at g = 3.71 m/s<sup>2</sup> with the lunar vehicles unchanged, 2,000 encounters per type and 12,000 for types 1 and 7, generated from E44's seeds so that each Mars encounter is paired with the lunar encounter of the same type, batch and index; and E43's ATC and uncoordinated cells at today's fleet, seeds 1–30 (the 2028 label marks the paired lunar runs; the Mars link uses no start year), with a Mars Earth link: round trips of 6, 20 and 44 minutes added to the two hours of staff time per referred conflict, Earth in view for the first 50 % of each sol (Assumed) or, as a variant, continuously through one areostationary relay, a 14-day conjunction from day 200 and two five-day dust storms, both as loss of the Earth link only. 44,000 encounters and 210 runs in seven cells.
P2-E47-GEOMETRY-SENTENCE: a second geometry on a Mars site was planned and not run, because the terrain reader is written for the lunar polar tiles and a Jezero base would need its own reader, sites and route network (Section 7).
P2-E47-INTRO-CLAUSE: On Mars, with the lunar vehicles on the same roads, the safety program behaved as on the Moon, the dead-stop exception included, but only on the flat: at Mars gravity the lunar brakes hold no downhill steeper than 7.7°, so no sloped encounter could be driven. Coordination that depends on Earth lost about one-sixth of what it loses on the Moon, the opposite of what we pre-registered for Mars (H9, Section 4.1): with Earth in view for half of every sol, as we assumed, a referred conflict waits hours, not the days of the polar base's window gaps (Section 5.8).
P2-E47-RESULTS-PARAGRAPH: The Mars part ran E44's twelve types at g = 3.71 m/s<sup>2</sup> with the lunar vehicles, 44,000 encounters paired with the lunar encounters of the same seeds, and E43's two road modes at today's fleet with a Mars Earth link (Tables 7 and 8). The safety program allowed no violation in eleven of the twelve types; in the dead-stop type the following vehicle closed below the required gap in 11 of 2,000 encounters, the same eleven encounters that violated on the Moon, and no vehicle touched another. With no violation the bound at 2,000 encounters is 2.7 × 10<sup>−3</sup> with the Bonferroni correction (1.5 × 10<sup>−3</sup> without), larger at the effective n of the weighted types; type 9's Clopper–Pearson limit is 1.2 × 10<sup>−2</sup> with the correction (9.1 × 10<sup>−3</sup> without), against 8.1 × 10<sup>−3</sup> (7.2 × 10<sup>−3</sup>) on the Moon at five times the sample. The ring deadlocked in 70 of 2,000 encounters (3.5 %, against 3.9 % on the Moon) and the landing closure twice in 2,000 (four in 10,000 on the Moon); no other type deadlocked. Of the 12,000 following draws, 8,961 (74.7 %) were on downhills steeper than 7.7°, the steepest the vehicles' 0.5 m/s<sup>2</sup> service brake holds at Mars gravity (Section 3.5), and were not driven; on the Moon the limit is 16.7–18.0° depending on the friction value, only the 20° draws are excluded, and 3,019 (25.2 %) of the same draws were not driven. No sloped encounter of any type was driven on Mars, and on the flat the braking term of R1 and R2 differs between the bodies by at most 0.01 m/s<sup>2</sup>, so the driven Mars encounters repeat the lunar ones with the same seeds. For the 4,411 paired encounters that nominal planners drove to the end on both bodies, the rules delayed the vehicles by 67.0 s on Mars and 66.9 s on the Moon, a ratio of 1.00. The logistics model's ATC mode uses neither gravity nor the Earth link, and its 30 Mars runs equalled E43's ATC runs on every seed. The uncoordinated mode cost 10.4 h [7.8, 13.1 h], 11.1 h [8.5, 14.0 h] and 10.8 h [8.8, 12.8 h] of delay per delivery above the ATC mode at round trips of 6, 20 and 44 minutes without a relay, and 8.2 h, 8.7 h and 6.4 h with the relay (Table 8); at 20 minutes without a relay that is 0.72 of the ATC mode's 15.5 h. On the Moon the same difference was 63.5 h [58.4, 68.9 h] in 2028, 4.1 times the ATC mode's delay, and 82.9 h [76.0, 89.7 h] in 2038 (Table 5); the Mars cost is 0.18 of the Moon's 2028 cost. The Mars fleet referred 94 conflicts a year to Earth and waited 772 h for the decisions, 8.2 h per conflict; the lunar fleet referred 53 and waited 1,969 h, 37.2 h per conflict. H9's first clause, zero violations under Mars gravity, is supported on the flat in the same eleven types as H7, fails in type 9 for the same encounters, and is untested on slopes; its second, a similar rule cost, is tested only by the encounter delays, where it holds; its third, that Earth-dependent coordination loses more on Mars, is contradicted: it loses less in every Mars cell, with intervals that do not overlap the Moon's.
P2-E47-DISCUSSION-CLAUSE: the safety program behaved as on the Moon, the dead-stop exception included, but that is weaker evidence than it looks: the only ground the lunar brakes hold at Mars gravity is nearly flat, and on the flat the braking term is the same on both bodies, so the Mars encounters that were driven repeat the lunar ones; the rules are untested on the slopes where Mars gravity acts. The same holds for the rules' cost, measured only by the paired encounter delays. The Earth-dependent mode lost about one-sixth of what it loses on the Moon, 11.1 h against 63.5 h, the opposite of H9's third clause. The reason is in the Earth windows, not the round trip: the three round trips gave the same cost within their intervals, and the relay lowered the mean at each, while a Mars base, as we modelled it, sees Earth for half of every sol (Assumed, Section 7) and the polar base's computed windows [42] leave it blind for days, so a referred conflict waited 8.2 h for a decision on Mars and 37.2 h on the Moon. The reversal therefore holds for any Mars site whose horizon returns Earth every sol, and would not for one that does not. The Mars fleet referred more conflicts (94 against 53) for the same demand and almost the same deliveries (2,932 against 2,928 items); we have not traced the cause. The one Mars-specific finding is about hardware. The guaranteed braking of Section 3.5 is the smaller of the service brake and the friction limit, less the downhill component: on the Moon the friction term binds at μ = 0.3 and the 0.5 m/s<sup>2</sup> service brake above it, so the holdable downhill is 16.7–18.0°; on Mars the service brake binds at every friction value, so braking does not grow with gravity while the slope term does, and the holdable downhill falls to 7.7°. Of the following draws, 75 % were on steeper ground, against 25 % on the Moon. R2 gives a zero admissible speed on such a slope, so the safety program refuses the slope; it has no rule that says a vehicle is under-braked for the body it is on, and vehicles for Mars need a service brake sized for Mars gravity.
P2-E47-LIMITATION-SENTENCE: The Mars part runs the same base, roads, routes and demand with Mars gravity, a Mars Earth link and the lunar vehicles, and its encounters repeat the lunar ones on the flat (Section 6.1); a Mars site with its own terrain, roads and vehicles was planned and not run, because the terrain reader is written for the lunar polar tiles; the share of each sol with Earth in view, the conjunction date and the dust storms are assumed, and the simulated year holds a conjunction, which comes once in about 26 months, a conservative choice; and at 2,000 encounters per type the Mars bounds are five times the Moon's for the same type, 2.7 × 10<sup>−3</sup> for the unweighted types with the Bonferroni correction and up to 6.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> for the weighted types (Table 7).
P2-H9-ABSTRACT-CLAUSE: On Mars the rules behaved as on the Moon, and referral to Earth cost about one-sixth as much.
P2-CONCLUSION-MARS-CLAUSE: On Mars the rules behaved as on the Moon and referral to Earth cost about one-sixth as much; at Mars gravity the lunar vehicles' brakes hold no downhill steeper than 7.7°.
